name: Diego Weber

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, and thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you tell me stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. There are no right answers. To start: tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm studying business management, and I live in a flat on Mill Lane with two lads from home. A normal week is lectures, a bit of study in the library, and then I drive back to Kellerton on Fridays to help in the shop. My family runs Weber and Sons, a hardware store, so I'm used to ordering stock and talking to customers. I like paper notes and a proper calculator. I don't use AI, and I haven't missed it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, because most of what I hear sounds like a sales pitch. In the shop we've heard about every new gadget and most of them end up in a drawer. I wouldn't argue about it, I'd just shrug.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means my life stays about the same. I'll finish the degree, go home and help run the shop, maybe grow it. My dad Franz says customers still want someone to find the right screw, and software can't do that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going to lectures and working Fridays at the shop. I might suggest we update the stock list from paper to a spreadsheet, because it's long overdue, but that's about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Honestly, it's what I expected. My family covers my costs, and the shop gives me a job whenever I want.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where would the spreadsheet come from?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd make it myself, in the plain kind of program we already have. I'm slow with new things, but a spreadsheet isn't scary. It's a list with sums.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you say when classmates talk about AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I nod and listen. I don't want to be the guy who says it's rubbish, because I don't know enough. I just don't feel the need to use it.

say: I'd say it sounds like a **sales pitch** and most gadgets end up in a drawer.
think: My life stays the **same**: finish the degree, then run the family shop.
Customers still want a **person** to find the right screw.
do: Keep going to **lectures** and working Friday shifts at the family shop.
Move the long paper stock list into a **spreadsheet** myself.
feel: **Calm**, because it is what I expected and the family covers costs.
S0.quote: I'm slow with new things, but a spreadsheet isn't scary. It's a list with sums.
fieldNote: **Resistance** is gentle: he's slow with new tools but not against them.
His family shop is his fallback and his plan.
Avoids debate because he does not know enough.

steps.text: Keep working Fridays at the family hardware shop
Move the paper stock list into a spreadsheet

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there'll be winners and losers, like with every change. I'd be pragmatic about it. If a tool saves time, use it. If it doesn't, don't. I wouldn't call it good or bad, I'd just see.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'm a bit uneasy. Business degrees are full of thinking work, like planning and checking and buying, and that's what the AI takes first. I might finish a degree that doesn't carry the same weight as it did for my uncle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably lean more on the shop. I'd learn the ordering part of the shop's software, slowly, with my sister Lena showing me. I'd also take practical modules in my degree, like accounting, because they feel solid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not scared, but the shop gives me a place to go, and I'd rather lean on that than gamble on a graduate job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why would your sister show you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She's two years older and works in the shop full time. She picks things up quick and she's patient with me. We argue, but she knows I get there in the end.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the shop feel safe?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Safer than an office job, yes. A robot can't carry a bag of cement into a customer's car. But the big chains can undercut us on price, and that worries my dad more than AI.

say: I'd say there will be **winners and losers**, like every change.
If a tool saves time, use it; if not, don't.
think: Business degrees are full of **thinking work**, which AI takes first.
The **shop** gives me somewhere to go instead of a graduate gamble.
do: Learn the shop's **ordering software** slowly with my sister Lena showing me.
Choose practical modules like **accounting** that feel solid.
feel: **Uneasy**, but not scared, because the shop is a fallback.
S1.quote: A robot can't carry a bag of cement into a customer's car.
fieldNote: Uses the **family shop** as his hedge against desk-job risk.
His fear is the big chains' prices as much as AI.
Learns with help from his sister rather than alone.

steps.text: Learn the shop's ordering software with my sister Lena
Take accounting and tax modules next term
Keep working shop shifts on Fridays and in the holidays

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's too fast and nobody's ready. I'd say governments should slow it down, though I doubt they can. I'd also say don't panic, because panicking helps no one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be frightened. The degree would be close to pointless, and even the shop would change, since the thinking side, ordering and prices, would go to software. Robots come three years later, so the shop has until about 2031. That gives my family a little time, but not much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably leave the course to work full time in the shop, to learn every part of it while there's still time. I'd talk to my dad Franz and sister Lena about whether to sell, keep going or change what we sell. I'd save every pound.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd lose sleep. I'd feel like I'd been carrying a plan that stopped working.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you really leave the degree?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If it's pointless, yes. I'd rather have three years of real work than three years of lectures on a world that's gone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about the three extra years for robots?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It gives the shop breathing room, but it's like being told your house will flood in 2031 rather than 2028. You still have to move.

say: I'd say it is **too fast** and nobody is ready, but not to panic.
I'd say governments should **slow it down**.
think: The degree could be **pointless** and even the shop's ordering would go to software.
Robots arrive three years later, so the shop gets only a little **time**.
do: Leave the course and work **full time** in the shop.
Talk to my family about whether to **sell or change** the shop.
feel: **Alarmed**, losing sleep over a plan that stopped working.
S2.quote: I'd rather have three years of real work than three years of lectures on a world that's gone.
fieldNote: Resistant to change, yet his answer is **decisive**: go back to the shop.
Reads the three-year robot gap as delay, not safety.
Fear is for the family business as well as himself.

steps.text: Leave the course and work full time at the shop
Save most of every pay packet
Sit down with Dad and Lena to decide whether to sell or change the shop

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is short, but it isn't the end of the world. I'd say people should wait and see how fast it really happens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd worry, but I'd feel I have time. I'd graduate in 2029, so there'd be two years of work before the thinking AI. I'd go home to the shop, learn the whole place, and be ready when the changes hit the till and the ordering.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree, because it's only three years. I'd work in the shop every holiday and learn the new ordering and stock systems, slowly. I'd save money so there's a cushion if the shop struggles.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'd have a plan, but it depends on the shop holding up and I can't control that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the shop doesn't hold up?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd look for a job in logistics or a trade company, somewhere with hands-on parts. I'd have to learn something fast, and I'm not good at that, but I'd do it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How's that different from the two-year version?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With five years I don't have to rush. I can finish the degree and wait to see. With two years I'd have no time to see.

say: I'd say five years is **short** but not the end, and people should wait and see.
think: I have **time** to finish the degree and learn the whole shop.
The plan depends on the **shop** holding up, which I can't control.
do: Finish the degree and work **every holiday** at the shop.
Save money as a **cushion** in case the shop struggles.
feel: **Anxious**: I have a plan, but it depends on things I can't control.
S3.quote: With five years I don't have to rush. I can finish the degree and wait to see.
fieldNote: The scenario rewards his **slow style**: waiting is possible with five years.
Names a backup in logistics, admits he is not quick to learn.
Anxiety comes from dependency on the shop.

steps.text: Finish the degree and work every holiday at the shop
Save part of the allowance each month as a cushion
Watch how the chains and the shop's suppliers change prices before deciding

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is long enough to do something sensible. I'd say we shouldn't make a fuss yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm fairly relaxed. I'd be 28, running the shop with my sister, maybe with a few new gadgets. There's time to learn slowly, and I'm better with slow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree and go into the shop, learn it end to end, and update it bit by bit. I'd also keep up some other skills, like accounting, in case the shop changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Ten years is more than enough to get used to anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if the shop was struggling in year eight?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd talk to my sister, and maybe sell it and put the money somewhere safe. It's family, so it's not a simple decision, but I'm not stubborn about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Anything you'd do differently if you had the extra time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably try a tool or two earlier. I just don't want to be first. I'd like to see it work in the shop before I put my name on it.

say: I'd say ten years is enough to do something **sensible** without a fuss.
think: I'd be **28**, running the shop with my sister and a few new gadgets.
There is time to learn slowly, and I'm better with **slow** change.
do: Finish the degree and go into the **shop**, learning it end to end.
Keep up **accounting** skills in case the shop changes.
feel: **Calm**: ten years is more than enough to get used to anything.
S4.quote: I'd like to see it work in the shop before I put my name on it.
fieldNote: Ten years suits his **cautious** nature perfectly.
Willing to sell the shop if it fails, which shows more flexibility than he claims.
Wants proof before he adopts anything.

steps.text: Finish the degree and move into running the shop with my sister
Keep up accounting skills in case the shop changes

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one. It's too quick for the shop, my family and me. What would help is a plan where small firms like ours get time and money to adapt, and people like my dad aren't left to cope alone. It'd also help if someone showed me, plainly, what the tools can do for a shop.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Just that I'm not as against all this as I sound. I'm just slow. I'd like to see something work before I trust it, and I'd like someone patient to show me.

headlineQuote: I'm not as against all this as I sound. I'm just slow.
portrait: Diego is a **business management student** who drives home on Fridays to work in his family's hardware shop.
He **never uses AI**, likes paper notes and a plain calculator, and prefers proof before he adopts anything.
Centre in outlook, he blames **nobody** in particular and treats change as winners and losers.
He is calm at a plateau and with ten years, but **alarmed** at 2028 and would leave for the shop.
The shop is both his **fallback** and his worry, because big chains can undercut it.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because the shop and his family have no time to adapt.
whatWouldHelp: A plan giving **small firms** time and money to adapt, and someone patient to show him what the tools do.
